## **Coursework 1 Brief**

At IIT, ATP runs as a **year-long module across two semesters**. **CW 1 is the Semester 1 coursework.** It assesses the team's understanding of the client problem, the requirements, the Agile way of working and the full design of the solution: the portfolio document with all UML and design diagrams, a high-fidelity prototype, a hosted landing page marketing website, and a presentation at the viva. Implementation of the product is the priority in Semester 2 and is not assessed in CW 1\.

Although CW 1 is documentation-focused, it must be produced the Agile way. The work is planned on a product backlog, delivered through Sprint 0 and Sprint 1, reviewed with the client and supervisor, and improved through retrospectives. Writing everything at the end and presenting it as sprints does not meet the requirements of this coursework. 

## **Learning Outcomes Assessed by CW 1**

**Table** 3**:** *Learning outcomes assessed by CW 1*

| Ref | Learning outcome |
| ----- | ----- |
| **LO1** | Analyse and interpret external client project specifications to identify clear functional and non-functional requirements. |
| **LO2** | Apply Agile methodologies and tools to plan, manage, and deliver software incrementally within a collaborative development team. |
| **LO3** | Design and prototype sustainable software solutions for the client project that demonstrate appropriate use of design principles, technologies, and user interface considerations. |
| **LO4** | Implement, test, and evaluate a software product meeting client and user needs, demonstrating good coding practice and software quality assurance. |

# **Assessment Components**

## **Weekly Supervision Meetings (Section A – 20 Marks)**

Every team is assigned a supervisor from the module team. Before the submission deadline, each team must attend **four mandatory weekly supervision meetings**, one per week. Each meeting is a feedback session and is marked out of 5 at the meeting itself, based on the team’s progress that week and the Agile practice it shows. This means the supervisor’s marks are complete before the submission, and the team receives feedback it can act on each week.

**Table** 4**:** *Weekly supervision meetings and marks*

| Ref | Meeting | What the team must show | Marks |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | :---: |
| A1 | **Meeting 1** – Sprint 0: Inception and Set-up | Agile framework chosen and roles assigned; team working agreement; task board and Git repository set up with the supervisor added; project brief understood; initial product backlog; draft release plan / roadmap. | 5 |
| A2 | **Meeting 2** – Sprint 0 Review and Sprint 1 Planning | Sprint 0 review and retrospective held and recorded; Sprint 1 goal and sprint backlog; requirement elicitation with the project under way; user stories with MoSCoW priority, estimates and acceptance criteria; risk register started. | 5 |
| A3 | **Meeting 3** – Sprint 1 Progress | Stand-ups recorded and burndown / burnup kept up to date; draft UML, architecture and wireframes; high-fidelity prototype in progress; backlog refined from project feedback; Sprint 0 retrospective actions followed up; landing page started. | 5 |
| A4 | **Meeting 4** – Sprint 1 Review and Draft Portfolio | Complete draft portfolio reviewed; prototype shown to the supervisor and feedback recorded; Sprint 1 review and retrospective; refined backlog and plan for Sprints 2 – 4; landing page live; presentation outline ready. | 5 |
| **Total** |  |  | **20** |

At every meeting the supervisor checks the live task board, the Git repository and the draft Google Document, and looks at:

* **Progress** – what the team has completed since the last meeting against its sprint goal and backlog.

* **Agile practice** – sprint planning, stand-ups, reviews and retrospectives held and recorded; the backlog and task board kept current with estimates, priorities and owners; burndown or burnup updated.

* **Use of feedback** – whether the feedback from the previous meeting has been acted on.

* **Preparation and teamwork** – an agenda and progress update brought to the meeting, minutes recorded in Appendix B, and every member contributing.

The meeting dates are agreed with the supervisor and recorded on the ATP Main document. A team that misses a meeting without approved mitigating circumstances receives 0 for that meeting. If a member misses a meeting the team attends, the supervisor may give that member a lower mark, with a written reason. The module team may moderate supervisor marks to keep them consistent across teams.

The weekly meetings mark the team’s progress. The **final version** of the Agile and project management work in the submitted portfolio (Chapter 3 and Chapter 7\) is assessed separately by the module team at the viva.

## **Individual Contribution**

CW 1 is a group submission and every team member must contribute to it. How individual contribution is verified, and the evidence each member provides, is set out in Chapter 8\. Individual contributions may be used to adjust individual marks.

## **CW 1 Deliverables**

By the deadline, each individual member submits the following through Blackboard and the Google Form:

* The portfolio document as a PDF, named 

  **\<IITID\_UoWID\_GroupNumber\_ATP\_CW1.pdf\>**

* The presentation slides as a PDF.

* Hosted Marketing website landing page \- eg sdgp.lk

* Links to the Google Document (view access, with version history, for the module team and supervisor), the Git repository, the task board, the high-fidelity prototype and the landing page website.

## **Presentation and Viva (B9 – 10 Marks, Individual)**

Each team has a viva slot of about 40 minutes: a presentation of about 10 minutes, followed by questions from two members of the module team. The viva schedule will be available on the ATP Main document. The presentation should cover:

* The project, the problem and the proposed solution, including what makes it unique. (WOW Factor)

* The Agile approach – roles, sprint structure and how the team has worked so far.

* Key requirements, user personas and the prioritised product backlog.

* The architecture and the most important UML and design diagrams.

* A live walkthrough of the high-fidelity prototype and the landing page website.

* Next steps and implementation progress

Every member must present part of the presentation and will be questioned individually on the portfolio and on their own contribution. Be ready to show the Google Document version history, the task board and the Git repository. The Presentation and Viva mark is awarded to each member individually. A member who is absent without approved mitigating circumstances receives 0 for this component.

## **Landing Page Marketing Website (B8 – 5 Marks)**

Every team must build and host a landing page marketing website for the product. Its purpose is to market the product to its target users – it is not the product itself. It must be live at the viva and must include:

* Product name, logo and a clear value proposition (headline).

* The problem and how the product solves it.

* Key features, with screenshots or mock-ups from the high-fidelity prototype.

* A team section (names and roles).

* Working call to action – for example a waitlist, pre-registration or contact form.

* Contact details, social links, & a privacy notice if any personal data is collected.

Technical requirements:

* Hosted on the team’s own .com or .lk domain over HTTPS. 

* Responsive on mobile, tablet and desktop, with no broken links.

* Accessible – alternative text for images, readable colour contrast and keyboard-friendly navigation.

* Basic search engine optimisation – page title, meta description, favicon and a social media preview image.

* Source code kept in the team Git repository. Adding analytics to show visitor numbers or sign-ups at the viva is encouraged.

# **Chapter 7: Sprint Records**

## **7.1 Chapter Overview**

| *This is a small introduction to your chapter.* |
| :---- |

This chapter records every sprint of the project, from Sprint 0 to Sprint 4, in one place. One record is completed per sprint using the same structure each time. Sprint 0 and Sprint 1 are delivered in Semester 1 and are fully recorded in Submission 1\. Sprints 2 – 4 are delivered in Semester 2; for Submission 1 only their goal, dates and planned backlog are completed.

**Table** 24**:** *Sprint overview*

| Sprint | Title | Semester | Status in Submission 1 |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Sprint 0 | Inception and Set-up | Semester 1 | Delivered – full record |
| Sprint 1 | Requirements and Design Increment | Semester 1 | Delivered – full record |
| Sprint 2 | \[Sprint title\] | Semester 1 | Planned – goal, dates and backlog |
| Sprint 3 | \[Sprint title\] | Semester 1 | Planned – goal, dates and backlog |
| Sprint 4 | \[Sprint title\] | Semester 1 | Planned – goal, dates and backlog |

Every sprint record uses the six sub-sections described below. Each sprint is numbered 7.x, so Sprint 0 is Section 7.2, Sprint 1 is Section 7.3, and so on.

**Table** 25**:** *Structure of each sprint record*

| Ref | Sub-section | What to include |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| 7.x.1 | **Sprint Goal and Dates** | The sprint goal and the start and end dates. |
| 7.x.2 | **Sprint Planning and Sprint Backlog** | The backlog items selected for the sprint, their estimates and owners (include a screenshot of the task board at sprint start). |
| 7.x.3 | **Stand-up and Progress Summary** | A summary of the stand-ups, blockers raised and how they were resolved, an events table, and a burndown or burnup chart with 3 – 5 sentences of interpretation. Detailed logs go in the appendix. |
| 7.x.4 | **Increment Delivered** | What was completed against the Definition of Done (for Sprint 1: requirements, design artefacts and prototype), with links to the repository, task board and prototype. |
| 7.x.5 | **Sprint Review and Feedback** | Feedback from the client, supervisor and users, and the changes it caused to priorities, scope or design. |
| 7.x.6 | **Sprint Retrospective** | What went well, what did not go well, and the improvement actions for the next sprint. Each retrospective must follow up on the actions agreed in the previous one. |

**Assessment tips**     

a) In the second year of your degree you should be able to resolve a lot of problems by yourselves. If you do get stuck, look at the later section about ‘managing issues’. Don’t go to your tutor for every question you could find the answer yourself; you are preparing to be independent professionals.  

b) Independent professionals who disappear and no one knows what they are doing, are not professionals and sooner or later get fired. Make sure your tutor knows what you are doing every week (i.e. attend tutorial slots).   

c) You should manage and complete the work as a team. You will have key points where you will show your work to your team-mates to get their feedback. There are more marks for a collegiate, helpful, behaviour to others (without doing their work for them\!) There will be marks lost for ignoring your team-mates, working in isolation, being late with your work, and so on.   

d) Identifying team issues early and managing them is an important part of the module. Minutes of meetings and agreements must also be updated online regularly for your tutor (tutor) to see but also as a record for the team of what you have discussed and agreed.

**Managing issues**  

All work, however well planned, can encounter something unexpected. It is important that you see such issues as learning opportunities and that you manage them, from beginning to end, professionally.   

To resolve an issue yourself:  

a) Do you have all the information about the problem? If not, try to find out the full story.  

b) Could you do something differently yourself and solve the issue? The success of the project will affect you so it is to your interest to adapt if you can.  

c) If the team needs to do something differently, can you convince the group what to do? How can you convince them that what you want will benefit them?  

Raising a case with your tutor:  

a) Have you exhausted the steps for resolving it yourself?  

b) Plan ahead what you want to ask and what you want from them (guidance? action? decision?).   

c) Be respectful of your tutor’s time. Your access to them is during the tutorial slot and only very exceptionally and if it is urgent by email.  

d) Be respectful to your colleagues. All resources are shared and limited, and that includes your manager/tutor. Ensure you are not asking for so much time that others will have to get little or nothing. (It’s actually unprofessional.)  

e) Separate private issues (e.g. “I have a doctor’s appointment next week” is something you should ask to discuss privately), from professional issues (“I'm not clear on how to do this”).  

f) Most of the times your tutor will not solve your problem but will try instead to help you solve it yourself, so you know how to do this in the future.  

Raising a case with your module leader:  

1) Any communication to the module leader must show that it has exhausted all avenues of resolving the issue yourself or with your tutor.

**What do you need to do to get a good mark?**  

Read this document carefully. Manage your work so that you do, typically, another 10 hours of work per week, outside lectures and tutorials. Go to lectures and go to tutorials as you can’t get anywhere else the help and information you need to do well. Seek feedback from your tutor and your teammates. Use that feedback to improve your work. Don’t miss what is on blackboard. Log on blackboard blog what you are doing. Polish your work: document well, write clearly, pay attention to the little details.  Always leave enough time to look at your work again and fix any missed errors.   

**What do you need to do to get a bad mark?**  

Read this quickly and expect someone else will tell you what you missed. Only do a couple of hours of work a week on this module. Don’t come to lectures expecting that you will pick things up from others or from blackboard. Write badly and submit work you did the night before the deadline. Ignore your team mates and their feedback – & give them low quality feedback in return. Assume that you can copy from someone else. Assume that the answer can be found on the internet (it cannot). Miss tutorials and the opportunity to get useful feedback from your tutor. Leave work for the last minute. Come to the presentation unprepared. Think that this is an easy coursework (it is not).  

**Managing issues**  

All work, however well planned, can encounter something unexpected. It is important that you see such issues as learning opportunities and that you manage them, from beginning to end, professionally.   

**Regulations**  

**Assessment regulations**  

Refer to part 3 of the Academic Regulations for a clarification of how you are assessed, penalties and late submissions, what constitutes plagiarism, etc.  

**Penalty for Late Submission**  

If students submit coursework late but within 24 hours of the published deadline, the work will be marked and will have ten percentage points of the overall available marks 

deducted, to a minimum of the pass mark (40% at undergraduate level). If students submit coursework more than 24 hours after the specified deadline, a mark of zero will be awarded for the work in question – unless a claim of Mitigating Circumstances has been submitted and accepted as valid.   

For more detailed information regarding University Assessment Regulations, please refer to the following website: [http\://www\.westminster.ac.uk/study/current-students/resources/academic-regulations](http://www.westminster.ac.uk/study/current-students/resources/academic-regulations%20%20)  

**Finally…**  There is nothing saying that you cannot do very well in this module. You all start with an equal chance to do very well, regardless of how you did last year. But how well you do is up to you and how professionally you are engaging with all aspects of the module. There is a lot of learning to be done with very interesting stuff directly related to how you survive in your future employment. Take it very seriously, but also try to enjoy it.
